subject: Mathematics
chapter_title: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 5 periods = 200 minutes
Total: 5 periods · 3h 20min

textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct triangles with these sidelengths (all in cm) using compass and ruler: (a) 4, 4, 6; (b) 3, 4, 5; (c) 1, 5, 5; (d) 4, 6, 8; (e) 3.5, 3.5, 3.5.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.1 p.150
textbook_items_in_class.description: Use points on a circle and/or its centre to form isosceles triangles (diagram given with one circle).

periods.activity_title: Swinging Arcs to Build Equal Sides

time_bands.activity: Students recall the Grade 6 method of finding a point equidistant from two endpoints using arcs. The teacher poses the question: if both arcs have the same radius as the base, what kind of triangle results? Students share predictions.

Students execute Construct, section 7.1 p.150 ("Construct triangles with these sidelengths using compass and ruler....") for cases (e) 3.5, 3.5, 3.5 first — the equilateral case — then cases (a) and (c) to observe how two equal sides emerge from equal arcs. The teacher circulates, checking that both arcs originate from the correct base endpoints.

Students examine Figure it Out Q1, section 7.1 p.150 ("Use points on a circle and/or its centre to form isosceles triangles...."). They identify which combinations of circle points produce equal radii and hence isosceles or equilateral triangles, articulating the reason in a brief written sentence.

Pairs share one finding each: which configuration gave an equilateral triangle and why. The teacher draws out the key idea — equal radii guarantee equal side lengths — and connects it to the arc-intersection logic used in the constructions.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often place the compass tip on the wrong endpoint when swinging the second arc, producing an asymmetric figure; a quick class check before students ink their constructions prevents this error. The arc-intersection logic — that C lies on both arcs and is therefore equidistant from A and B — is the idea to press on, not just the finished shape.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.1 p.150
homework.description: Use points on two (or three) equal circles and/or their centres A, B (and C) to form isosceles and equilateral triangles.

textbook_segments.title: Constructing a Triangle When its Sides are Given

textbook_items_in_class.description: Attempt to construct triangles with sidelengths 3 cm, 4 cm, 8 cm and 2 cm, 3 cm, 6 cm. Find more sets of lengths for which a triangle is impossible, and identify a pattern.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.154
textbook_items_in_class.description: Without constructing: could you have determined that 3, 4, 8 cm and 2, 3, 6 cm cannot form triangles? Explain using the triangle inequality.

For any set of three lengths, will at least two comparisons always satisfy 'direct length < sum of other two'? Explore. Also find which length can be identified as immediately less than the sum without calculation.

periods.activity_title: When Arcs Miss: Discovering the Triangle Inequality

time_bands.activity: The teacher reminds students that the two-arc method (established in equilateral triangle construction) depends on the arcs actually intersecting. The class is asked: what happens to the arcs if one side is very long?

Students attempt Math Talk, section 7.2 p.151 ("Attempt to construct triangles with sidelengths 3 cm, 4 cm, 8 cm and 2 cm, 3 cm, 6 cm....") in pairs. They record whether their arcs intersect and describe what they observe when they do not. They then generate two further failing sets and look for a numerical pattern.

Class discussion surfaces the pattern. Students then tackle Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.154 ("Without constructing: could you have determined that 3, 4, 8 cm and 2, 3, 6 cm cannot form triangles?....") to articulate the triangle inequality as a checking rule.

Students investigate Try This Q3, section 7.2 p.154 ("For any set of three lengths, will at least two comparisons always satisfy 'direct length < sum of other two'?...."). Groups share which comparison is always satisfied and why the longest side is the only one to check against the sum of the other two.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common reasoning error here is checking only one pair (e.g., just the longest side against one other side) and missing the full statement; press students to articulate all three comparisons before concluding. The tent-tree-pole metaphor from the textbook — a direct path is shorter than any detour — is a productive verbal anchor when students struggle to explain why the inequality must hold.

textbook_segments.title: Constructing a Triangle When its Sides are Given

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.156
textbook_items_in_class.description: Which sets of lengths can be sidelengths of a triangle? Explain: (a) 2, 2, 5; (b) 3, 4, 6; (c) 2, 4, 8; (d) 5, 5, 8; (e) 10, 20, 25; (f) 10, 20, 35; (g) 24, 26, 28.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.159
textbook_items_in_class.description: Check if a triangle exists for: (a) 1, 100, 100; (b) 3, 6, 9; (c) 1, 1, 5; (d) 5, 10, 12.
For each pair of given sides, find at least 5 valid values for the third side: (a) 1, 100; (b) 5, 5; (c) 3, 7. Describe all possible third-side values for each case.

periods.activity_title: Checking and Constructing with the Triangle Inequality

time_bands.activity: The teacher revisits the triangle inequality rule established through the arc-failure experiments: for a triangle to exist, the longest side must be less than the sum of the other two. Students state the rule aloud before applying it.

Students work through Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.156 ("Which sets of lengths can be sidelengths of a triangle?....") individually, writing a one-line justification for each case. The teacher listens for students who identify the longest side correctly before comparing.

Students check Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.159 ("Check if a triangle exists for: (a) 1, 100, 100....") and compare answers with a partner. The borderline case (b) 3, 6, 9 is brought to whole-class discussion: the arcs touch at exactly one point, producing a degenerate triangle.

Students explore Try This Q3, section 7.2 p.159 ("For each pair of given sides, find at least 5 valid values for the third side....") for one chosen pair. They express the range of valid third-side values as an inequality and share their generalisation with the class.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent slip is accepting a degenerate case (sum exactly equal, not strictly greater) as a valid triangle; highlight case (b) of the p.159 exercise as the canonical example of this boundary. Students who finish the range exploration early can be asked to express the valid third-side interval using inequality notation, connecting the geometric reasoning to algebraic form.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.2 p.154
homework.description: Determine whether triangles exist for: (a) 10 km, 10 km, 25 km; (b) 5 mm, 10 mm, 20 mm; (c) 12 cm, 20 cm, 40 cm.

textbook_segments.title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given

textbook_items_in_class.description: Do triangles always exist for every combination of two angles and the included side? Find examples where they do not.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.165
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the third angle (using a parallel-line argument) when two angles are: (a) 36°, 72°; (b) 150°, 15°; (c) 90°, 30°; (d) 75°, 45°.

Exterior angle: find ∠ACD if ∠A = 50° and ∠B = 60°. Then find the exterior angle for different ∠A and ∠B values and derive the relationship between the exterior angle and the two non-adjacent interior angles.

periods.activity_title: Angle Sums, Parallel Lines, and When Arms Never Meet

time_bands.activity: The teacher presents the parallel-line proof of the angle-sum property: draw XY parallel to BC through A, identify the alternate angles ∠XAB = ∠B and ∠YAC = ∠C, and note that the three angles form a straight angle at A. Students reconstruct each step in their notebooks.

Students apply the angle-sum property in Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.165 ("Find the third angle using a parallel-line argument when two angles are...."), writing the subtraction step explicitly. The teacher brings case (b) 150° + 15° to attention: the sum already exceeds 180° once the third angle is sought.

Math Talk, section 7.3 p.162 ("Do triangles always exist for every combination of two angles and the included side?....") is discussed in pairs. Students produce examples where the two base angles are supplementary (arms become parallel) and where their sum exceeds 180° (arms diverge), explaining in geometric terms why C cannot be located.

Students work on Figure it Out, section 7.3 p.166 ("Exterior angle: find ∠ACD if ∠A = 50° and ∠B = 60°...."), deriving the exterior-angle theorem from the angle-sum property. They state the relationship as a general rule in their own words.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently confuse an exterior angle with its adjacent interior angle; directing attention to which angles are non-adjacent to the exterior angle prevents this. The deductive chain — parallel postulate → alternate angles → straight angle at vertex → angle sum — is worth tracing aloud so students see each step's logical dependence on the one before it.

textbook_segments.title: Constructions Related to Altitudes of Triangles

textbook_items_in_class.description: Altitudes Using Paper Folding: cut out a paper triangle, fix one side as the base, and fold so the crease is the altitude from the top vertex to the base. Justify why the crease is perpendicular to the base.
Visualise and draw a rough diagram: in what type of triangle is a side also an altitude?
Construct the altitude from A to BC using ruler and set square, for the given triangle (extended base case shown also).

periods.activity_title: Folding and Drawing the Perpendicular Drop

time_bands.activity: Students perform Activity, section 7.4 p.168 ("Altitudes Using Paper Folding: cut out a paper triangle, fix one side as the base, and fold so the crease is the altitude...."). Each student folds their own triangle and justifies in one sentence why the crease must be perpendicular to the base.

Students consider Figure it Out, section 7.4 p.168 ("Visualise and draw a rough diagram: in what type of triangle is a side also an altitude?...."). They sketch rough diagrams and identify the right-angled triangle as the case where a leg is itself an altitude, explaining in terms of the perpendicularity condition.

Students construct the altitude using ruler and set square as described in Figure it Out, section 7.4 p.169 ("Construct the altitude from A to BC using ruler and set square...."), including the extended-base case where the foot of the altitude falls outside the triangle. The teacher demonstrates the set-square alignment before students begin.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often draw the altitude to the nearest side rather than the correct base, and in acute triangles this matters because all three altitudes lie inside; in the extended-base case, confusion about where to extend BC is common — show the extension explicitly before students draw. The paper-folding step is not merely decorative: the crease's perpendicularity can be justified because folding maps the two half-planes onto each other, and students who articulate this have understood the definition of altitude.

items.prompt: A triangle has all three sides equal. Which of the following correctly describes this triangle using both classification systems?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A — Equilateral and acute-angled. Each angle of an equilateral triangle equals 60° (since 180° ÷ 3 = 60°), which is acute, so the triangle is both equilateral (by sides) and acute-angled (by angles).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the angle-sum property: equal sides force equal angles, and 180° ÷ 3 = 60°, which is acute.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student knows the side classification but incorrectly assigns a right angle; may believe any symmetric triangle can have a 90° angle without checking the angle sum.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student confuses equilateral with isosceles (equilateral is a special case of isosceles, but the more precise label is equilateral); angle classification is correct.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has not connected equal sides to equal angles and has not applied the angle-sum property — likely confusing classification labels.

inclusivity.support: Let the student look up the definitions of equilateral, isosceles, and scalene in their textbook, then measure one constructed equilateral triangle's angles to confirm each is 60°.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to explain in their own words why an equilateral triangle can never be right-angled or obtuse-angled, using the angle-sum property as their argument.

items.section_title: Constructing a Triangle When its Sides are Given
items.prompt: A student claims that any three lengths can be used to construct a triangle as long as all three are positive. Give a specific counter-example with three positive lengths and explain, using the arc-intersection idea, why the construction fails for your example.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Counter-example: 2 cm, 3 cm, 8 cm. The longest side is 8 cm, but 2 + 3 = 5 < 8. When constructing, the arc of radius 2 cm from one base endpoint and the arc of radius 3 cm from the other do not reach each other — they fall short of intersecting — so no point C can be found and the triangle cannot be built.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the triangle inequality: if the longest side is not less than the sum of the other two, the two arcs do not intersect and the triangle cannot exist.

inclusivity.support: Encourage the student to actually attempt the construction with compass and ruler for their counter-example, observing that the arcs fall short, before writing the explanation.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to alter the counter-example by changing only the longest side so that the three lengths just barely satisfy the triangle inequality, and describe what the arc diagram looks like in that borderline case.

exercise.description: Attempt to construct triangles with sidelengths 3 cm, 4 cm, 8 cm and 2 cm, 3 cm, 6 cm. Find more sets of lengths for which a triangle is impossible, and identify a pattern.

items.prompt: Using compass and ruler, construct an equilateral triangle with side length 5 cm. Write down the three steps of your construction procedure and state the length of each side of the completed triangle.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Step 1: Draw base AB = 5 cm. Step 2: Set compass to 5 cm and draw an arc centred at A. Step 3: Without changing the compass width, draw a second arc centred at B; mark point C where the two arcs intersect. Join AC and BC. Each side (AB, AC, BC) equals 5 cm because C lies on both arcs, each of radius 5 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw a 5 cm base, swing equal arcs of 5 cm from both endpoints, and mark C at the intersection — each side equals the arc radius.

inclusivity.support: Provide a partially completed diagram showing base AB already drawn, and ask the student to add only the two arcs and mark C.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to construct a second equilateral triangle sharing side AC with the first, and describe what shape the two triangles together form.

items.section_title: Constructing a Triangle When its Sides are Given
items.prompt: Determine which of the following sets of side lengths can form a triangle. For each set, show the key inequality check. Sets: (a) 7 cm, 11 cm, 15 cm; (b) 4 cm, 9 cm, 14 cm; (c) 6 cm, 6 cm, 11 cm.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) Longest side = 15; check 7 + 11 = 18 > 15. Triangle exists. (b) Longest side = 14; check 4 + 9 = 13 < 14. Triangle does not exist. (c) Longest side = 11; check 6 + 6 = 12 > 11. Triangle exists.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the longest side and check whether it is strictly less than the sum of the other two; if yes, a triangle exists.

inclusivity.support: Provide a visual number line or comparison strip showing the three lengths side by side so the student can see whether the two shorter lengths together reach the longest.
inclusivity.challenge: For set (a), ask the student to find two different values for a fourth side length that would make a new valid triangle with 7 cm and 11 cm, and express all valid values as an inequality.

exercise.description: Which sets of lengths can be sidelengths of a triangle? Explain: (a) 2, 2, 5; (b) 3, 4, 6; (c) 2, 4, 8; (d) 5, 5, 8; (e) 10, 20, 25; (f) 10, 20, 35; (g) 24, 26, 28.

items.section_title: Constructions Related to Altitudes of Triangles
items.prompt: A triangle has vertices at three points on your paper. Describe the set-square-and-ruler steps to construct the altitude from the top vertex to the base. Then state what is special about the altitude in a right-angled triangle.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Steps: (1) Align the ruler along the base BC. (2) Place the set square so that one leg lies along the ruler. (3) Slide the set square along the ruler until its vertical edge passes through vertex A. (4) Draw the line segment from A to the point where the vertical edge meets BC (or its extension) — this is the altitude. In a right-angled triangle, one of the two legs is itself an altitude because it is already perpendicular to the other leg, which serves as the base.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Align ruler to the base, slide the set square until its perpendicular edge reaches the vertex, and draw the segment — in a right-angled triangle one leg is the altitude to the other.

inclusivity.support: Provide a printed triangle and ask the student to physically place a set square on the ruler, slide it, and trace the altitude before writing the steps.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to construct all three altitudes of a given acute triangle using the same method and describe where the three altitudes appear to meet.

exercise.description: Construct the altitude from A to BC using ruler and set square, for the given triangle (extended base case shown also).

dropped_units.activity_title: Classifying Triangles by Sides and Angles

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces the two classification systems for triangles — by sides (equilateral, isosceles, scalene) and by angles (acute, right, obtuse) — and asks students to place the triangles they have already constructed into both systems simultaneously. Students propose combinations and assess whether each is geometrically possible.

Students construct and classify Figure it Out Q1, section 7.5 p.170 ("Construct triangle ABC with BC = 5 cm, AB = 6 cm, CA = 5 cm. Construct the altitude from A to BC...."). They name it by sides, then measure its angles to determine its angle classification, recording both labels.

Students investigate Figure it Out Q4, section 7.5 p.170 ("Explore whether it is possible to construct: a right-angled equilateral triangle; an obtuse-angled equilateral triangle; a right-angled isosceles triangle; an obtuse-angled isosceles triangle....") through attempted construction or angle-sum argument. They explain why (a) and (b) are impossible using the angle-sum property.

Students attempt Try This Q3, section 7.5 p.170 ("Construct right-angled triangle ∆ABC with ∠B = 90° and AC = 5 cm...."), discovering that infinitely many such triangles exist because only the right angle and hypotenuse are fixed. Students articulate what additional information would pin down a unique triangle.

dropped_units.teacher_notes: Students commonly believe that classifying by sides and by angles are independent systems — the exploration in Figure it Out Q4 is the moment to make explicit that an equilateral triangle is necessarily acute, using the angle-sum property (each angle must equal 60°). Watch for students who incorrectly claim a right-angled equilateral triangle is possible by misapplying the 90° condition to one angle without checking the sum.
